hints: Look at what is attacking the iodoethane, water provides a nucleophile, not an electrophile, so think about which substitution fits haloalkanes.
The C-I bond breaks and $OH^-$ from water replaces iodine, releasing $I^-$ ions into solution for the silver ions to find.
Recall your silver halide colours in order, chloride is white, bromide is cream, so work out what iodide must be.
walkthrough:
**Identify the organic reaction type**

Haloalkanes like $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{I}$ undergo substitution by nucleophiles. Here water provides $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and $\text{OH}^-$ to replace the halogen.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{I} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH} + \text{H}^+ + \text{I}^-$$

**Follow the released halide ion**

The $\text{C-I}$ bond breaks heterolytically to give $\text{I}^-$ in solution. This is the classic hydrolysis test for haloalkanes, warmed with aqueous silver nitrate.

$$\text{Ag}^+(aq) + \text{I}^-(aq) \rightarrow \text{AgI}(s)$$

**Recall the silver halide precipitate colour**

Silver halide colours get darker down Group 17. $\text{AgCl}$ is white, $\text{AgBr}$ is cream, and $\text{AgI}$ is yellow.

Since iodide is released, we get a yellow precipitate of $\text{AgI}$. Nucleophilic substitution plus yellow matches one row exactly.

options.A: Incorrect on both parts. Haloalkane hydrolysis is nucleophilic substitution, not electrophilic substitution, and cream is the colour of AgBr, not AgI.
options.B: Half right but the mechanism is wrong. Yellow is correct for AgI, but electrophilic substitution is for arenes like benzene, not for attack on a haloalkane by water.
options.C: The reaction type is correct, but the colour is wrong. Cream precipitate indicates bromide ions and AgBr. Iodoethane releases iodide, which gives yellow AgI.
options.D: Correct. Water acts as a nucleophile replacing I in a nucleophilic substitution (hydrolysis), and the released I- forms yellow AgI precipitate with Ag+.
